flawed_step: The claim that 'beats' is transitive. Nontransitive dice show it can fail.
counterexample: Let X, Y, Z be independent. X is uniform on {2,4,9}, Y is uniform on {1,6,8}, and Z is uniform on {3,5,7}. No two of them can ever be equal, so there are no ties. P(X>Y) = (1/3)(1/3 + 1/3 + 1) = 5/9 > 1/2, because 2 beats only 1, 4 beats only 1, and 9 beats all three. P(Y>Z) = (1/3)(0 + 2/3 + 1) = 5/9 > 1/2, because 1 beats nothing, 6 beats 3 and 5, and 8 beats all three. P(Z>X) = (1/3)(1/3 + 2/3 + 2/3) = 5/9, because 3 beats 2, 5 beats 2 and 4, and 7 beats 2 and 4. So P(X>Z) = 1 - 5/9 = 4/9 < 1/2. X beats Y and Y beats Z, but X does not beat Z.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. A counterexample is a set of nontransitive dice: three independent uniform variables on {2,4,9}, {1,6,8} and {3,5,7}. X beats Y and Y beats Z, each with probability 5/9, but P(X>Z) is only 4/9.
